stories.title: The Girl Who Caught the Clouds

pages.text: Every morning in the mountains near Abha, the fog rolled into the valley like a slow white tide. Fourteen-year-old Layla liked to watch it from her grandfather's terrace while the rest of the house was still asleep. Below them, the coffee trees on the lower terraces had been struggling for months, because the rains had come late again. "If only we could drink the clouds," her grandfather said, half joking, as he poured the qahwa. Layla didn't laugh, because the idea had already stuck in her mind.

That afternoon she noticed a spider's web glittering between two branches, heavy with tiny drops. Although it hadn't rained for weeks, the web was soaking wet. She crouched down and watched one drop slide along a thread and fall onto a leaf below. Suddenly, everything clicked. The fog wasn't just passing through the valley; it was carrying water that nobody was catching.

The school's annual invention fair was only six weeks away, and Layla had been searching for a project ever since it was announced. Her older brother Omar was sceptical. "A net that catches water from the air? You'll be the laughing stock of the whole school." "People laughed at the first aeroplane too," Layla replied, rolling her eyes. With her mother's permission, she borrowed some fine plastic mesh, two wooden poles and a length of old pipe from the shed.

Her first prototype was simple: the mesh was stretched between the poles, with a pipe underneath leading into a bucket. She set it up on the edge of the terrace before bed, too excited to sleep properly. At dawn she rushed outside, only to find the net ripped and the bucket lying on its side, completely empty. A strong gust in the night had torn the whole thing apart. Omar didn't say a word, but his raised eyebrows said everything.

Layla was tempted to give up, but her grandfather took her for a walk instead. He led her to a crumbling stone wall at the far end of the farm, built long before he was born. "My grandfather told me these walls were built facing a particular direction," he explained, running his hand over the damp stones. "They face the wind, so the fog leaves its water on them, and the water runs down to the roots." Layla stared at the wall in amazement, realising that her ancestors had solved the same problem centuries ago.

Inspired, she redesigned her invention from scratch. This time she angled the net to work with the wind rather than fight it, and she secured the frame with heavy stones, just like the old wall. She also added a second layer of mesh, having read that a double layer traps more drops. Even Omar, who had stopped teasing her, offered to help dig the posts into the ground. The next morning the bucket held almost four litres of clear, cold water, and Layla let out a cry of delight that woke half the house.

By the day of the fair, the improved design had been collecting water every morning for three weeks. Layla presented it alongside photos of the stone wall and a chart showing exactly how much water she had gathered. One of the judges, an engineer from the university, asked her a question she hadn't expected. "Did you invent this, or did you discover it?" Layla hesitated, then answered honestly: "Both, I think. My great-great-grandparents had the idea first; I've just found a new way to use it."

When the results were announced, first prize went to a boy who had built a robot that sorted rubbish. Layla clapped for him sincerely, though she couldn't help feeling a little disappointed. Afterwards, however, the engineer came to find her. "The university is studying ways to bring water to mountain farms," she said. "Would your family let us test a larger version of your nets on your terraces?" Layla was so stunned that, for once in her life, she was lost for words.

By the following spring, a row of tall nets stood along the top of the farm, glittering every morning like enormous spider webs. The coffee trees had turned green again, and two neighbouring farmers had already asked for nets of their own. Layla's grandfather sat on the terrace, pouring the qahwa as usual. "So," he said with a smile, "you really did teach us to drink the clouds." "No, Jiddo," Layla said, looking out at the old stone wall. "We just remembered how."

pages.text: Noura had always thought that her grandfather's study smelled of old paper and cardamom. Three months after he passed away, she was helping her father sort through his shelves when a small leather notebook slipped out and landed at her feet. Inside, in faded blue ink, was a diary of a road trip he had taken to Oman in 1978. Tucked between the last two pages was a brass compass, its glass scratched but its needle still trembling towards the north. On the final page, Grandfather had written just one sentence: "One day, I must return this to Salim."

"Who on earth is Salim?" Noura asked, turning the compass over in her hands. Her father shook his head slowly, because he had never heard the name before. They read the diary together that evening, and the story gradually came to life. As a young man, Grandfather had been caught in a sandstorm while driving through the mountains, and his car had broken down near a tiny village. A shepherd called Salim had found him, given him water and dates, and lent him this compass so that he could find his way to the nearest town.

"He kept it for more than forty years," her father murmured. "He must have felt terrible that he never managed to give it back." Noura studied the hand-drawn map inside the cover, with its wobbly lines and the name of a village: Al-Qarn. Before she could stop herself, she said, "Why don't we take it back for him?" To her surprise, her father didn't laugh; instead, he smiled the way Grandfather used to when he was planning something.

Two weeks later, during the school holidays, Noura and her parents set off in the family car with the diary on Noura's lap. She had taken charge of navigation, comparing Grandfather's notes with the map on her phone. The modern highway was smooth and fast, nothing like the rough tracks he had described, and she couldn't help wondering how frightened he must have been. At the border, the officer flicked through their passports and asked about the purpose of their visit. "We're returning something that was borrowed," Noura replied, and the officer raised his eyebrows with a puzzled smile.

Finding the village turned out to be far harder than they had expected. Al-Qarn didn't appear on any online map, and the first three people they asked had never heard of it. By the second afternoon, as the car climbed narrow roads between steep, rust-coloured cliffs, Noura was beginning to feel they were looking for a needle in a haystack. Then she noticed a lonely fig tree beside a dry riverbed, exactly like the one sketched in the diary. "Stop the car!" she shouted. "Grandfather drew this tree!"

Beyond the tree, a dusty path led to a cluster of stone houses clinging to the mountainside. An elderly man in a white dishdasha was sitting outside a small shop, and he watched them curiously as they approached. Noura's father greeted him politely and explained, a little nervously, why they had come. The man listened in silence, but when Noura held out the compass, his eyes widened. "That belonged to my father," he said quietly. "My name is Hamad, and I am Salim's son."

Hamad invited them into his home, where his wife served coffee in tiny cups along with a plate of sweet dates. He explained that Salim had passed away ten years earlier, but he had often told the story of the young Saudi traveller lost in the storm. "My father always said the man would come back one day," Hamad said, shaking his head in wonder. "We used to tease him about it, because we thought the stranger had simply forgotten." Noura felt a lump in her throat as she realised that both old men had remembered each other for a lifetime.

When Noura placed the compass in Hamad's hands, he turned it over gently, just as she had done in Grandfather's study. Then, to everyone's surprise, he pushed it back towards her. "My father lent it so that a traveller could find his way," he said. "Now it has guided you all the way here, so it belongs with someone who still has many journeys ahead of her." Noura tried to refuse, but Hamad insisted, and her father gave her a small nod to show that she should accept.

Before they left, Hamad's family made them promise to visit again, and Noura wrote their address carefully inside the diary. On the long drive home, she held the compass up to the window and watched the needle settle steadily towards the north. She realised that the trip had never really been about returning an object; it had been about finishing a story that Grandfather had started. Now, she thought, the next chapter was hers to write. Under Grandfather's final sentence, she added one line of her own: "Returned, and given back again."

pages.text: Faisal Al-Harbi had always loved football, but at fifteen he had discovered something he loved even more: refereeing. While his friends dreamed of scoring goals, he studied the rules until he knew them by heart. Every Friday after prayers, he watched matches with a notebook and wrote down every decision he would have made differently. His father found it strange at first, but eventually he bought Faisal a proper black whistle. "If you're going to do this," he said, "do it properly."

After months of training courses in Riyadh, Faisal was chosen to referee the final of the city's under-16 tournament. It was an enormous honour, especially for someone so young. However, when he saw the team list, his heart sank. The captain of Al-Nakheel Academy was his cousin Majed, who had practically grown up in the same house as him. Faisal wondered whether he should ask to be replaced, but his coach, Ustadh Saleh, told him that a good referee never runs away from a difficult situation.

On the night of the final, the stadium was packed with families waving scarves and flags. Faisal's grandmother was sitting in the front row, and he could tell from her proud smile that she expected great things from both of her grandsons. During the warm-up, Majed jogged past and winked at him. "Don't forget who taught you to ride a bike," he joked. Faisal laughed, but the comment stayed in his mind like a stone in his shoe.

The first half was fast and fierce, and Faisal had to keep his cool as players argued over every throw-in. He showed two yellow cards, one to each side, so nobody could accuse him of being unfair. At half-time the score was 1–1, and the crowd was getting louder by the minute. In the changing room, Faisal splashed cold water on his face and reminded himself of his father's words. Tonight he was not anyone's cousin; he was the referee.

With three minutes left and the score still level, Al-Waha's striker broke through the defence. Majed raced back and threw himself into a desperate tackle inside the penalty area. The striker fell, and thousands of people jumped to their feet at once. Faisal had been perfectly positioned, and he had seen it clearly: Majed had caught the player's ankle, not the ball. For a second, the noise seemed to disappear, and he could hear only his own heartbeat.

Faisal blew his whistle and pointed firmly to the penalty spot. The Al-Nakheel players surrounded him, shouting that he had made a terrible mistake. Majed stared at him in disbelief, his face red with anger. "Are you serious?" he demanded. "You know I'd never tackle like that!" Faisal said nothing; he simply showed him a yellow card and calmly asked the players to step back.

The striker scored, and Al-Waha won the cup. As the winners celebrated, Faisal walked off the pitch without looking at the stands, convinced that half the stadium hated him. He hardly slept that night, replaying the moment in his head again and again. By the next morning, he was dreading the family lunch at his grandmother's house, where Majed would certainly be waiting.

When Faisal arrived, his cousin was sitting in the majlis with his phone in his hand. Without a word, Majed showed him a video filmed from the stands and slowed down frame by frame. It proved that his boot had struck the striker's ankle. "I've watched it twenty times," Majed admitted, looking embarrassed. "I was wrong to shout at you. If you had let it go, I'd always have known the cup wasn't really ours."

A week later, a letter arrived from the regional football association. Faisal had been selected for the national youth refereeing programme, partly because an observer had praised his "courage and calm under pressure" in the final. At lunch, his grandmother asked Majed what he thought of the news. Majed grinned and put an arm around his cousin's shoulders. "He's the toughest referee I've ever played against," he said, "and the fairest."

stories.title: The Iron Road and the Old Guide

pages.text: In the summer of 1908, the whole city of Madinah was talking about one thing: the iron road. For years, workers had been laying tracks across the desert from Damascus, and now the Hejaz Railway was almost complete. Fourteen-year-old Hamza could hardly sleep at night, imagining the great black engine rolling into the new station. His grandfather, Saleh, however, was far from impressed. "I have guided caravans through this desert for forty years," he grumbled. "No smoking monster will ever understand the sand the way a camel does."

Hamza had been running errands at the station for months, and the station master, Mr. Kamal, had taken a liking to him. He had even shown Hamza how the telegraph worked, tapping messages along the wire that followed the tracks. "Messages travel faster than any rider," Mr. Kamal explained, "as long as the line stays up." That evening, Hamza tried to share his excitement at dinner, but his grandfather simply shook his head. "Machines are clever," the old man said, "but the desert is cleverer."

A week before the grand opening, Saleh had to collect dates from a village to the north, and he asked Hamza to come along. They set off before dawn on two of the family's camels, following an ancient route that ran close to the new railway. Around midday, his grandfather suddenly stopped and stared at the horizon. The sky had turned a strange yellow colour, and the air felt heavy and still. "Get down," he ordered calmly. "A storm is coming, and it won't wait for us."

They led the camels behind a group of large rocks and made them kneel, then wrapped their scarves tightly around their faces. Within minutes, the wind was howling and the sun had completely disappeared. Hamza pressed himself against the warm side of his camel, his heart pounding. Through the roar, he could hear his grandfather reciting verses from the Quran in a steady voice, and gradually his fear began to fade. The storm raged for nearly three hours before it finally blew itself out.

When they climbed out, the landscape looked completely different. Hamza ran to the top of a small hill and gasped. Below them, in a narrow cutting between two ridges, the railway had vanished under a huge new dune. Worse still, the telegraph pole beside it had been knocked flat, and its wire lay buried in the sand. "The afternoon train from the north is due to pass here before sunset," Hamza whispered. "If the driver doesn't see the sand in time, the whole train could come off the rails."

For a moment, neither of them spoke, and Hamza realised that no message could warn anyone now. Then his grandfather placed a firm hand on his shoulder. "My knees are too old for a fast ride, but yours are not," he said. "Follow the tracks north, but cut across the dry valley where the line bends, and you will save an hour." He pulled off his red headscarf and pressed it into Hamza's hands. "Wave this as if your life depends on it, because other lives certainly do."

Hamza rode harder than he had ever ridden before, his camel's long legs eating up the ground. By the time he crossed the valley, the sun was sinking fast and his throat was burning with thirst. Then he saw it: a thin column of black smoke rising in the distance. He drove his camel up onto the tracks, stood up in the saddle and waved the red scarf wildly above his head. With a terrible screech of metal, the engine slowed, and finally came to a stop only a few metres in front of him.

The driver jumped down, red-faced and furious, but his anger disappeared once Hamza had explained what lay ahead. Soon, passengers and crew were walking south together, carrying every shovel the train had on board. When they reached the cutting, they found Saleh already there with a dozen men from the nearby village, who had seen the storm and come to help. Working side by side under the rising moon, they cleared the track before midnight. The driver shook the old man's hand warmly. "You and your grandson saved us all tonight," he said.

On the first of September, when the railway was officially opened, Mr. Kamal called Hamza and his grandfather to the front of the crowd to thank them in front of everyone. Hamza noticed that his grandfather was watching the shining engine with a new kind of respect. "Perhaps this monster is not so bad," Saleh admitted with a smile, "but it still needs a camel now and then." Years later, Hamza became one of the first engineers from Madinah to work on the line. Whenever young workers asked him for advice, he always gave the same answer: "Trust your machines, but never stop listening to the desert."

pages.text: Every Eid, the whole family gathered at Grandma Noura's house in Taif, and every Eid, her chicken kabsa was the star of the meal. This year, however, Grandma had flown to Riyadh to visit Aunt Huda, and she was supposed to be back by noon. At ten o'clock, Faisal's phone buzzed with a message that made his stomach drop: "Flight delayed. Start the kabsa without me. The notebook is in the top drawer." Faisal was fourteen and had never cooked anything more complicated than an omelette. He stared at the screen in disbelief.

His sister Lama, who was sixteen and considered herself the sensible one, found the notebook within seconds. It was a battered old thing with a cracked leather cover, and its yellowed pages were covered in Grandma's curly handwriting. They quickly turned to the page marked "Kabsa for thirty," and Lama groaned. At some point, someone had spilled a whole cup of tea across it, and half of the ingredients had faded into a brown blur. "We can read 'rice', 'chicken' and 'onions'," she said, "but the spices have completely disappeared."

Faisal tried calling Grandma, but the call went straight to voicemail, which meant her phone had either died or been switched off for the flight. Thirty guests were expected at two o'clock, and the kitchen suddenly felt enormous and unfriendly. "We could just order from a restaurant," Faisal suggested, though he already knew what Lama would say. "And tell Grandma her Eid kabsa was replaced by a takeaway? Not a chance." She tied her hair back, washed her hands and handed him an apron.

They began with what they could read: the onions, which Faisal chopped with streaming eyes, and the chicken, which Lama browned in Grandma's huge pot. When it came to the spices, though, they hit a wall. The spice cupboard held at least twenty jars, many of them unlabelled, and both of them were reluctant to guess. Then Faisal had an idea. "Close your eyes," he said, "and try to remember what the kitchen smells like when Grandma is cooking."

Feeling slightly ridiculous, Lama did as he said, and after a moment a faint smile crossed her face. "Cardamom," she said slowly, "definitely cardamom, and something warm, like cinnamon." Faisal opened jar after jar, sniffing each one carefully, until he found a small dark one that made him laugh out loud. Inside were dried black limes, the bitter, smoky loomi that Grandma always dropped into the pot whole. "I'd recognise that smell anywhere," he said. "It's the smell of every Eid I can remember."

By midday, the pot was bubbling away and the kitchen smelled almost, but not quite, right. Something was missing, and neither of them could work out what it was. They argued about adding more salt, then about cumin, until Lama threw up her hands and declared that too many cooks spoil the broth. "There are only two of us," Faisal pointed out, and they both burst out laughing despite their nerves. Then he remembered something: before every big meal, Grandma heated a dry pan, and the house filled with a sweet, nutty smell.

"She toasts the whole spices first!" Lama cried. "That's what we've forgotten!" They toasted cardamom pods, cloves and coriander seeds until the smell flooded the room, and this time they both knew immediately that it was right. At two o'clock sharp, the doorbell began to ring, and uncles, aunts and cousins poured into the house. Faisal and Lama carried out large platters of golden rice and chicken, topped with fried almonds, trying to look far calmer than they felt. There was still no sign of Grandma.

Just as everyone was sitting down, the front door opened and Grandma walked in, tired but smiling, having arrived in the nick of time. She sat down without a word, took a spoonful of kabsa and chewed thoughtfully while the whole room fell silent. "This isn't my kabsa," she said at last, and Faisal's heart sank. Then her eyes began to shine. "It's yours," she continued, "and I'm almost sorry to say it's very nearly better than mine."

Later, Faisal showed her the ruined page and apologised for the tea stain. To his surprise, Grandma laughed. "That page was never much use, habibi. I stopped measuring things forty years ago, and I cook with my nose and my memory, exactly as you two did today." She took a pen, turned to a fresh page and wrote in her curly handwriting: "Kabsa by Faisal and Lama, to be cooked again next Eid." Faisal smiled, realising that the most important ingredients had never been written in any notebook at all.

dialogue.t: Do you think teenagers spend too much time on their phones?

Really? Why do you say that?
The main reason I feel this way is that I lose hours scrolling through videos instead of sleeping.
I know what you mean. Not only does it keep me up late, but it also makes me tired in class.
Exactly. And social media can be really addictive, especially with all the notifications.
Still, I use it to keep in touch with my friends, so I don't think it's all bad.

grammar.title: Not only ... but also (with inversion)

dialogue.t: I think the school should ban phones in class completely. They're nothing but a distraction.

Some do, but wouldn't it be better if teachers decided when phones could be used?
Hmm, that sounds like a lot of work to enforce. A total ban is simpler.
Simpler, maybe, but a ban doesn't teach us to use technology responsibly.
That's a good counterargument. So what compromise would you suggest?
Phones stay in our bags unless the teacher says we need them for a task.

dialogue.t: So, which do you prefer: online learning or being in a real classroom?

True. Whereas online learning lets you rewatch lessons, classroom learning gives you instant feedback.
And there's more interaction in class. I felt a bit of isolation when we studied online.
Me too, although I liked not having to wake up so early!

dialogue.t: Do you think there should be stricter rules on fast food adverts for young people?

Thanks, I kept looking at my notes. I'll practise it a few more times.

grammar.title: Signposting Language in Presentations
grammar.ar: عبارات الإرشاد (signposting) تساعد المستمع على متابعة أجزاء العرض: المقدمة والجسم والخاتمة. نستخدم Today I'd like to talk about لتقديم الموضوع، ويأتي بعد Let me start by فعل بصيغة ing. ونستخدم Moving on to للانتقال إلى فكرة جديدة، ويأتي بعدها اسم أو فعل بصيغة ing، ثم To wrap up لتلخيص الأفكار وإنهاء العرض.
examples: Today I'd like to talk about why I love photography.
Let me start by showing you the first photo I ever took.
Moving on to the equipment, you don't actually need an expensive camera to begin.

words.ex: There was a sharp rise in the number of teens using social media at night.
The chart shows a slight drop in reading time between 2020 and 2023.
Over half of the respondents said they sleep less than seven hours a night.
Time spent gaming increased gradually over the five-year period.
The number of students who exercise daily remained steady throughout the year.
There is a significant difference between how much boys and girls read.

dialogue.t: Let's look at this chart about teenagers' sleep. What do you notice first?
According to the chart, most teens slept around eight hours a night in 2019.
Right, but look at what happened after that.
There was a slight drop in 2020, and then a sharp rise in screen time at night in 2021.
And sleep went down to about six and a half hours. That's a significant change.
This suggests that phones and gaming are affecting how much teens sleep.
I agree, although the chart doesn't prove it directly. Other factors like homework could also matter.
Good point. We should mention that in our analysis.

grammar.title: Describing Trends: Nouns and Verbs
grammar.ar: يمكن وصف التغيّرات في الرسوم البيانية بطريقتين: باستخدام صفة + اسم مثل There was a sharp rise، أو باستخدام فعل + ظرف مثل The number rose sharply. ونستخدم According to the chart لنسب المعلومة إلى مصدرها. أما This suggests that فنستخدمها لتقديم تفسير أو استنتاج دون أن نؤكده تأكيداً تاماً.
examples: There was a sharp rise in gaming hours between 2019 and 2022.
Reading time dropped slightly among students aged fifteen and sixteen.
This suggests that teenagers prefer digital entertainment to books.

words.ex: Our team has five minutes to pitch our idea to the school principal.
A school garden would benefit students by teaching them about healthy food.
We want a sustainable project that continues after we graduate.
The project has a small budget, so we'll need to find sponsors.
The teachers asked whether the plan was feasible within one term.
She addressed the parents' concerns about safety very clearly.

dialogue.t: Good morning, everyone. The idea behind this project is to start a book exchange corner in our school library.
This would benefit students by giving them free access to books and encouraging them to read more.
Thank you. I have a question: how would you make sure the books come back?
That's a great question — what I mean is that it's an exchange, not a loan. You take a book only if you bring one.
I see. And who would organise it every week?
We already have six student volunteers, and the librarian has agreed to supervise.
It sounds feasible. Would you need any budget?
Very little — just some shelves and labels. We'd raise the money with a bake sale.

grammar.title: Using 'would' for Proposals
grammar.ar: عند تقديم فكرة مشروع لم يُنفَّذ بعد، نستخدم would + الفعل في صيغته الأساسية لأننا نتحدث عن نتائج متوقعة أو افتراضية. وفي عبارة This would benefit ... by ... يأتي بعد by فعل بصيغة ing لشرح الطريقة. ونستخدم That's a great question — what I mean is ... للرد على الأسئلة بلباقة وتوضيح ما قصدناه.
examples: This would benefit younger students by giving them older mentors to talk to.
The recycling bins would reduce plastic waste in the cafeteria.
That's a great question — what I mean is that volunteers would only work one hour a week.

words.ex: We can only speculate about why they are all standing on the roof of the car.
Her facial expression shows that she's more surprised than scared.
Judging by his body language, he's feeling quite relaxed.
The boy on the right looks puzzled, as if he doesn't understand what's going on.
In the background, you can see some people running towards the building.
Apparently, they've been waiting there for quite a long time.

dialogue.t: Look at this photo. They might be waiting for help because the water around the car is really deep.
Maybe, but it looks as if they're actually enjoying it. They're all laughing!
True. The man in the middle can't be scared. He's clearly making a joke about the whole thing.
What about the girl on the left? She looks a bit puzzled to me.
She might be a tourist because she's taking photos of everything around her.
And look at the sky in the background. It looks as if the rain has just stopped.
So they can't be in real danger anymore. They're clearly just waiting for the water to go down.
Exactly. I'd say they're making the best of a bad situation.

grammar.title: Present Deduction: might, can't, must & It looks as if
grammar.ar: نستخدم might أو could عندما نخمّن شيئًا ممكنًا لكننا غير متأكدين، وcan't عندما نكون متأكدين أن الشيء غير صحيح، وmust أو clearly عندما نكون شبه متأكدين أنه صحيح. يأتي بعد هذه الأفعال المصدر مثل be أو be + فعل ينتهي بـ ing. أما It looks as if فتتبعها جملة كاملة (فاعل + فعل) لوصف ما يبدو من الصورة. لاحظ أن عكس must في الاستنتاج هو can't وليس mustn't.
examples: They might be a family on holiday because they're carrying lots of suitcases.
It looks as if the woman has just received some good news.
He can't be a professional photographer. He's clearly using his phone camera.

words.ex: The disappearance of the crew is still unexplained after 150 years.
There's no real evidence that pirates attacked the ship.
One popular theory is that a sudden storm hit the area.
The whole crew seemed to vanish without leaving a single message.
That's the most plausible explanation I've heard so far.
Divers discovered the shipwreck near the coast of the Red Sea.

dialogue.t: Have you heard about the Mary Celeste? It was found floating in the Atlantic in 1872 with nobody on board.
Nobody at all? It must have been pirates, surely.
But nothing was stolen. The cargo and the crew's belongings were all still there.
Then maybe there was a storm. They could have got into the lifeboat instead of staying on the ship.
That's one theory. But there's no way they would have left a safe ship unless they thought it was about to sink.
Wasn't the cargo alcohol? Strong fumes could have made them think it was going to explode.
Exactly. That sounds the most plausible to me. They must have panicked and then got lost at sea.
It's a bit scary to think we'll probably never know for sure what happened.

grammar.title: Past Deduction: must have, could have, would have
grammar.ar: للتخمين حول أحداث وقعت في الماضي نستخدم: must have + التصريف الثالث للفعل عندما نكون شبه متأكدين، وcould have أو might have + التصريف الثالث عندما يكون الأمر محتملًا فقط، وcan't have + التصريف الثالث عندما نكون متأكدين أنه لم يحدث. وتُستخدم there's no way they would have ... unless ... لنقول إن شيئًا ما مستحيل إلا بشرط معيّن. انتبه: نقول must have gone وليس must have went.
examples: The ancient city must have been destroyed by a huge sandstorm.
They could have travelled by sea instead of crossing the desert.
There's no way they would have left their gold behind unless they were in serious danger.

words.ar: مُستدام / صديق للبيئة على المدى الطويل
words.ex: NEOM aims to be one of the most sustainable cities in the world.
Qiddiya is one of the giga-projects connected to Vision 2030.
By 2040, most of our electricity might come from renewable energy like solar power.
I'd love to ride in a driverless taxi through Riyadh.
AlUla has become a popular tourist destination for visitors from all over the world.
The country is investing billions in new roads, railways and other infrastructure.

dialogue.t: What do you think Saudi Arabia will be like in 2040?
By 2040, we'll probably have driverless taxis in every major city. The Riyadh Metro is already running, after all.
True. And it's likely that The Line in NEOM will have thousands of residents by then.
Maybe, but I doubt that it will be completely finished. It's such a huge project.
Fair point. What about tourism? I think the Red Sea resorts will be famous all over the world.
Definitely. It's likely that millions of tourists will visit AlUla and Qiddiya every year.
And it's unlikely that people will still drive petrol cars, don't you think?
I'm not so sure. I doubt that everyone will switch to electric cars that quickly, but renewable energy will probably power most homes.

grammar.title: Future Predictions with Degrees of Certainty
grammar.ar: عند التنبؤ بالمستقبل نُظهر مدى تأكدنا باستخدام تعبيرات مختلفة. نضع probably بعد will (we'll probably have) لكن قبل won't (we probably won't). ونستخدم It's likely / unlikely that + جملة كاملة للحديث عن احتمال مرتفع أو منخفض، وI doubt that ... will ... عندما لا نصدّق أن شيئًا سيحدث. وتعني By 2040 «بحلول عام 2040»، أي قبل ذلك التاريخ أو عنده.
examples: By 2040, we'll probably have flying taxis between Riyadh and Jeddah.
I doubt that people will stop visiting traditional markets completely.
It's unlikely that the desert will disappear, but it's likely that we'll see more green spaces in our cities.

words.ex: If I were the principal, I'd let students have a longer break.
I think the curriculum should include more practical skills like coding.
Our timetable is so packed that we barely have time to breathe.
Extracurricular activities like debate clubs help students build confidence.
Students often complain that their homework workload is too heavy.
Even small changes to the school day could make a big difference.

dialogue.t: If you were the principal for a day, what would you change?
The first thing I'd do is start school an hour later. Most of us are half asleep in the first lesson.
Ha, I'd vote for that! If I were the minister of education, I would reduce the homework workload.
Interesting. But suppose students could choose all their own subjects. What would happen?
I think they'd be more motivated, although some might just pick the easiest ones.
Good point. If I were in charge, I'd also add more extracurricular activities, like robotics and debate clubs.
And I'd make sure every school had a proper sports hall. That would really make a difference.
Sounds like we'd make a great team. Maybe we should send our ideas to the principal!

grammar.title: Second Conditional & Suppose
grammar.ar: نستخدم الجملة الشرطية الثانية للحديث عن مواقف خيالية أو غير مرجّحة في الحاضر أو المستقبل: If + الماضي البسيط، ثم would + المصدر. في الأسلوب الرسمي والصحيح نقول If I were مع جميع الضمائر بدلًا من was. ويمكن استخدام Suppose + الماضي البسيط لطرح فكرة خيالية، ثم نسأل what would happen? لاحظ أن الفعل بعد If يكون في الماضي رغم أن المعنى عن الحاضر.
examples: If I were the minister of education, I would make coding a compulsory subject.
The first thing I'd do is give every student a tablet.
Suppose students could design their own timetable, what would happen?

words.ex: I really regret not taking part in the school trip last year.
When I look back on that day, I realise I overreacted.
Things turned out much better than I expected.
I missed the chance to meet my favourite author because I arrived late.

words.ar: بعد فوات الأوان / عند النظر إلى ما حدث
words.ex: In hindsight, choosing that subject was a great decision.
I forgot my passport once, and I definitely learned my lesson.

dialogue.t: Is there any decision you'd make differently if you could go back?
Yes. Last year I quit the football team because I thought it took up too much time. I wish I hadn't done that.
Really? What happened?
Well, they won the regional championship. If I had stayed, I would have played in the final.
That's tough. For me, it was the science fair. Looking back, I should have started my project much earlier.
Did it turn out badly?
Not terribly, but if I had planned better, I would have had time to test it properly. I definitely learned my lesson.
Same here. Next time I'll think twice before giving up on something.

grammar.title: Third Conditional, wish + Past Perfect & should have
grammar.ar: نستخدم الجملة الشرطية الثالثة للحديث عن ماضٍ لم يحدث ونتائجه الخيالية: If + الماضي التام (had + التصريف الثالث)، ثم would have + التصريف الثالث. ونعبّر عن الندم على شيء فعلناه أو لم نفعله في الماضي بـ I wish + الماضي التام. أما should have + التصريف الثالث فتعني «كان يجب أن...» ولكننا لم نفعل. انتبه: لا نستخدم would بعد If في الجزء الأول من الجملة.
examples: If I had studied harder, I would have passed the exam easily.
I wish I hadn't said those things to my best friend.
Looking back, I should have listened to my parents' advice.

words.ex: Choosing between two friends' parties was a real dilemma for me.
If I found a phone in the mall, I'd hand it in to security.
I'd feel guilty if I kept money that wasn't mine.
I promised to help him, so I don't want to let him down.
It's hard to turn down an invitation from a close friend.
The trip sounds fun. On the other hand, I have an important exam the next day.

dialogue.t: Okay, here's a dilemma. You find a wallet with 500 riyals in it, but there's no ID card. What would you do?
In that situation, I'd probably hand it in to the police, as long as the station wasn't too far away.
Really? Some people would just keep it.
Unless I knew for sure that nobody would claim it, I wouldn't keep a single riyal. I'd feel too guilty.
Fair enough. What about this one? Two friends invite you to their events on the same evening.
It depends on whether one of them is a special occasion, like a graduation.
Let's say one is a birthday and the other is a graduation party.
Then I'd go to the graduation, as long as I could explain it to my other friend. I wouldn't want to let anyone down without telling them.

grammar.title: Conditions with as long as, unless & it depends on whether
grammar.ar: نستخدم as long as بمعنى «بشرط أن»، وunless بمعنى «إلا إذا» أي if not، لذلك لا نضع بعدها فعلًا منفيًا (نقول unless I knew وليس unless I didn't know). وتُستخدم It depends on whether ... للقول إن القرار يعتمد على أمر معيّن قد يكون صحيحًا أو لا. وعند الحديث عن مواقف خيالية نستخدم الماضي البسيط بعد هذه الروابط مع would في الجزء الآخر من الجملة.
examples: In that situation, I'd probably tell the teacher, as long as my friend didn't get into serious trouble.
Unless I had a really good reason, I wouldn't turn down my cousin's wedding invitation.
It depends on whether the owner's phone number is inside the wallet.

units.t: Making Your Case: Opinions and Debate
units.cando: I can develop a clear argument on topical issues, giving reasons for and against a point of view and responding to counter-arguments politely and convincingly.
lessons: Screens and Teens
Discuss whether teenagers spend too much time on smartphones and social media, giving personal examples and reasons
While it's true that ..., I'd argue that ...; The main reason I feel this way is that ...; Not only does it ..., but it also ...
School Rules Under Review
Debate a proposed school rule (banning phones in class, longer school days) with the teacher taking the opposite side
I see your point, but have you considered ...?; That may be the case, however ...; Wouldn't it be better if ...?
Online vs. Classroom Learning
Compare the advantages and disadvantages of online and in-person learning and reach a balanced conclusion
On the one hand ..., on the other hand ...; Whereas online learning ..., classroom learning ...; All things considered, I'd say ...
Fast Food Nation
Argue for or against stricter rules on fast food advertising aimed at young people, using facts and examples
There's growing evidence that ...; It could be argued that ...; If we don't ..., there's a risk that ...
Agreeing to Disagree
Practise conceding points and politely maintaining your position in a heated discussion about sports or e-sports as real sport
I'll admit that ..., but I still believe ...; You've got a point there, although ...; Let's just say we see it differently because ...
Mini-Debate Showdown
Take part in a structured mini-debate: opening statement, rebuttal and closing summary on a teen-relevant motion
I'm firmly in favour of / against ... because ...; My opponent claims that ..., yet ...; To sum up, the strongest argument is that ...

units.cando: I can speculate about causes, consequences and hypothetical situations, expressing different degrees of certainty about the past, present and future.
lessons: Reading the Picture
Look at a photo of people in an unusual situation and speculate about who they are, what is happening and how they feel
They might be ... because ...; It looks as if ...; She can't be ... — she's clearly ...
Mysteries of the Past
Discuss an unexplained event or historical mystery and suggest possible explanations
It must have been ...; They could have ... instead of ...; There's no way they would have ... unless ...
Saudi Arabia in 2040
Imagine life in Saudi Arabia in 2040 with new cities, technology and tourism linked to Vision 2030 projects
By 2040, we'll probably have ...; I doubt that ... will ...; It's likely / unlikely that ...
If I Were in Charge
Discuss what you would change if you were the school principal or the minister of education for a day
If I were ..., I would ...; The first thing I'd do is ...; Suppose students could ..., what would happen?
Regrets and Second Chances
Talk about a past decision you would make differently and how things might have turned out
If I had ..., I would have ...; I wish I hadn't ...; Looking back, I should have ...
The Big Dilemma
Work through moral and practical dilemmas (finding a lost wallet, choosing between friends' events) and justify your choices
In that situation, I'd probably ... as long as ...; Unless ..., I wouldn't ...; It depends on whether ...

units.t: Speaking with Impact: Stories and Presentations
units.cando: I can give clear, well-structured descriptions, narratives and short presentations on a range of topics, highlighting key points and supporting them with relevant details.
lessons: A Story Worth Telling
Narrate a memorable experience (a trip to AlUla, a family Eid gathering, a competition) with vivid detail and suspense
I had been ... for hours when suddenly ...; Just as we were about to ..., ...; It was only later that I realised ...
How It Works
Explain a process clearly, such as how to prepare Saudi coffee or how a favourite app works
The first step is to ...; Once that's done, ...; It's essential to ... otherwise ...
People Who Inspire
Describe an inspiring person (a scientist, athlete or family member) and explain their influence on you
What I admire most about ... is ...; Despite ..., he/she managed to ...; He/She has taught me that ...
Structuring a Talk
Plan and deliver a 2-minute talk on a hobby or interest using a clear introduction, body and conclusion
Today I'd like to talk about ...; Let me start by ...; Moving on to ...; To wrap up, ...
Data and Trends
Describe a simple chart about teen habits (sleep, reading, gaming) and comment on what the data shows
According to the chart, ...; There was a sharp rise / slight drop in ...; This suggests that ...
My Project Pitch
Present an idea for a school or community project and handle questions from the audience
The idea behind this project is ...; This would benefit ... by ...; That's a great question — what I mean is ...

units.t: Exam-Ready Speaking: B2 First and IELTS
units.ar: الاستعداد للامتحان: محادثة B2 First و IELTS
units.cando: I can perform confidently in B2 First and IELTS-style speaking tasks, extending answers fluently, comparing ideas and discussing abstract topics with appropriate language.
lessons: First Impressions Count
Practise interview-style questions about home, studies, free time and future plans, extending answers beyond one sentence
Well, to be honest, ...; What I really enjoy is ... because ...; In the future, I'm hoping to ...
Comparing Photos
Complete a one-minute long turn comparing two photos (e.g., studying alone vs. in a group) and answering the follow-up question
Both pictures show ..., but in the first one ...; The people here seem more ... than ...; I'd imagine they're ... because ...
The Cue Card Challenge
Speak for two minutes on an IELTS Part 2 topic card, such as a place you'd like to visit, after one minute of planning
The place I'd like to talk about is ...; What makes it special is ...; I'd love to go there because ...
Working Together
Complete a B2 First collaborative task: discuss options with the teacher and negotiate a final decision
Shall we start with ...?; What do you think about ...?; I'm not sure that's the best option, how about ...?; So we've agreed that ...
Thinking Bigger
Answer abstract Part 3 / Part 4 discussion questions on education, technology and society with developed reasoning
Generally speaking, ...; This is partly because ... and partly because ...; In contrast, older generations tend to ...
Full Mock Exam
Complete a full mock speaking test with timing, then receive feedback on fluency, vocabulary, grammar and pronunciation
That's an interesting question, let me think ...; What I mean to say is ...; Could you repeat the question, please?; Another point worth mentioning is ...
